overview: A safety management system is a structured way for an organization to spot hazards, manage risks, check that safety measures work, and build a safety-minded culture. This bill requires the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to create an independent expert panel within 60 days to review how well the agency's own internal safety management system works across its offices, including air traffic control, aviation safety, and airports. The panel would include experts from NASA, representatives of pilots', air traffic controllers', and safety inspectors' unions, independent safety experts, and airline and aerospace industry staff, with nonvoting members from the National Transportation Safety Board and the U.S. mission to the International Civil Aviation Organization (the UN body that sets global aviation standards). It would also review the FAA's voluntary safety reporting programs and its compliance with international standards. Within 180 days of first meeting, the panel would issue a public report of findings and recommendations, and the FAA would have to brief Congress on its progress and publicly explain any recommendation it rejects. As of September 14, 2026, it had been approved by a Senate committee and placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say the FAA requires airlines to run strong safety systems and should be held to the same standard, and an outside review with frontline workers involved can find weaknesses before they lead to accidents.
against: Critics say another review panel adds reporting work for an agency already stretched thin, and the FAA can reject the panel's recommendations, so real improvement still depends on the agency's follow-through.
